lessons.title: Festivals and Occasions
lessons.summary: Unit 1 explores festivals in Kuwait and around the world. Students read about the Hala February Festival and the Qurain Cultural Festival, listen to descriptions of festivals (National Day, a carnival, Losar) and of the Hajj, practise modal verbs of ability, intensifiers and phrasal verbs with 'go', and plan an imaginary community festival.

readings.title: Hala February Festival in Kuwait
readings.summary: Kuwait's most dazzling annual celebration, launched in 1999, takes place in spring and coincides with National Day (25 February) and Liberation Day (26 February). It mixes culture, entertainment, shopping, carnivals, raffles and contests, and attracts tourists, especially families from the Gulf. The desert turns green and migratory birds arrive. Shops offer huge discounts, making it an important economic event, but spreading joy and patriotism is most important to its organisers.

readings.title: Cherry Blossom time in Japan (Workbook)
readings.summary: Cherry Blossom festivals take place all over Japan in March or April. Viewing the blossom has been a custom since at least the 7th century CE (some historians claim the 3rd century). The festival marks the beginning of spring and the start of the academic and financial years. People hold parties called hanami and eat dango, a chewy snack made of rice flour, from home or street vendors. Tokyo's parks and Kyoto's historical areas are popular. The cherry blossom is Japan's national flower; there are over 400 types of cherry tree (Sakura), which do not produce fruit. Meteorologists track the Sakura Zensen, the warm weather front that makes the trees blossom.

grammar.topic: Modal verbs of ability: can / could / be able to / manage to
rules: can / can't + base form: ability in the present.
could / couldn't + base form: general ability in the past.
be able to: used to make other tenses (present perfect, future).
managed to / was able to: ability on ONE particular occasion in the past, often something difficult (NOT could).
couldn't is usually used for negative sentences, both general and particular.
examples: I could swim when I was four years old. (general ability)
The door was locked, but we managed to get out by breaking a window. (particular occasion)
I haven't been able to walk since I broke my leg. (present perfect)
I hope I'll be able to see better with my new glasses. (future)

rules: Intensifiers (quite, really, very, a little, pretty, brand, fairly, extremely, absolutely) modify adjectives and adverbs, not usually verbs.
They come before the word they modify.
'absolutely' goes with extreme (non-gradable) adjectives: absolutely impossible / terrified / astonished / perfect / exhausted.
'very' goes with ordinary (gradable) adjectives: very difficult / frightened / surprised / good / tired.
examples: The film was quite good.
You are absolutely right.
They got a brand new car.
He was extremely surprised.

rules: go + adverb/preposition creates a new meaning.
examples: go out = stop burning/shining: The lights went out.
go on = continue: This went on for about ten minutes.
go away = leave for a holiday: We're going away for two weeks.
go up = increase: The price of bread has gone up.
go off = ring (alarm) / explode: My alarm clock goes off at six.
go under = sink: The ship went under at three o'clock.
go against = oppose: I can't go against my father's wishes.
go through = experience something difficult

rules: Past simple: completed past actions; generally true or repeated past actions.
Past continuous: background activities; an action in progress when something else happened.
examples: Turks brought coffee to Constantinople in 1453.

readings.title: Grandmother celebrates her return from Hajj

After collecting her from the airport, Grandma explained she had always dreamed of the Hajj and had finally achieved her life-long aim. After a long breakfast, the family invited close relatives for a special meal. Mum had decorated the house. grammar.topic: Simple past and past perfect (once / when / before / after / by the time)
rules: Form: had + past participle (had had, hadn't eaten, Where had they lived?).
Use the past perfect for the FIRST of two past actions; the simple past for the later one.
Use it to explain a situation or feeling in the past: They were hungry because they hadn't eaten.
Time words: after, before, as soon as, once, when, by the time.
Inversion: No sooner had ... than ...; Hardly had ... when ...
examples: As soon as we had eaten breakfast, we invited our close family over.
By the time we finished the meal, Grandma had begun to tell us about her experience.
No sooner had Ahmed woken up than the phone rang.
By the time I went to bed, I had been to school and done my homework.

rules: Compound noun = noun + noun; the first noun acts like an adjective (bathroom, hairbrush, chair leg).
Derivatives are formed with suffixes such as -ion, -or, -ant, -al.
examples: lunch + time = lunchtime; birth + day = birthday; tea + pot = teapot; grand + father = grandfather; fire + works = fireworks; neck + lace = necklace; free + lance = freelance

celebrate → celebration; decorate → decoration/decorator; congratulate → congratulation; collect → collection/collector; participate → participant; arrive → arrival; invite → invitation; visit → visitor

readings.summary: 1000 CE: the Galla people in Ethiopia ate coffee beans for energy; Arab traders imported coffee and boiled the beans to make qahwa. 1453: coffee arrived in Istanbul. 1652: the first coffee house opened in London. 1690: the Dutch took coffee to Ceylon and Java. 1901: the first instant coffee. 1903: decaffeinated coffee invented. 1946: the espresso machine invented in Italy. 1971: the first big chain of coffee shops opened.

readings.title: Coffee houses
readings.summary: Today business people use the Internet for news; 300 years ago they went to coffee houses to read newspapers, catch up on news, hear lectures, do business and chat. Early European coffee houses (1650s) were for businessmen, writers, politicians and scientists; only men went, because people thought coffee was bad for women's health. Coffee was first grown in Ethiopia, where people chewed the beans, then spread to Arab countries as a drink. Pasqua Rosee from Smyrna, Turkey, opened London's first coffee house in 1652. Coffee houses became the centre of social life: calm, pleasant places where anyone who started a quarrel had to buy coffee for everyone. In other European countries coffee was first drunk as a medicine. In Kuwait, serving coffee is at the heart of hospitality; in the Diwaniya conversations and transactions happen over Kuwaiti coffee ground with cardamom. A guest's cup is refilled until he tips the empty cup from side to side.

readings.title: Tea - a daily necessity (Workbook)
readings.summary: Tea is the most popular drink in the world. Its cultivation began in China over 2,000 years ago and spread to Japan (6th century CE) and Arab countries (9th century CE). With silk and porcelain it is one of China's main exports. In China everyone drinks tea, especially after meals; people believe it keeps them cool in summer, and the elderly meet in tea-houses. Tea shows respect, accompanies apologies, and in weddings the bride and groom serve their parents tea in gratitude and receive a red envelope for good luck. 40 countries grow tea, 90% in Asia; a skilled picker collects 600 g a day.

rules: Form: If + past perfect, would (not) have + past participle.
Use: imagined (unreal) situations in the past and their imagined results.

rules: Zero: If + present, present - things that always happen: If it rains, we get wet.

readings.title: The Diwaniya
readings.summary: Diwaniyas are informal social gatherings, usually of Kuwaiti men, to discuss anything from business and football to politics and literature. 'Diwaniya' means a place of assembly; it comes from the Arabic 'diwan', the office where the Amir meets his subjects. Traditionally held in a large tent with cushions, it now usually has permanent structures. Family Diwaniyas reinforce ties in extended families; since the 18th century major families built an extension to their house for guests, weddings and funerals, often in a U-shape with elders at the head. Politicians hold Diwaniyas to meet constituents and voters, a tradition dating back to the first Amir, Sabah the First, who visited Diwaniyas to learn of public grievances. Women often hold their own gatherings at the same time. The Diwaniya preserves Kuwait's time-honoured culture.

readings.title: Communication Breakdown
readings.summary: People spend over 75% of their time in interpersonal situations, so poor communication causes many personal problems. Effective communication, especially listening, is essential for healthy relationships. A major source of problems is defensiveness: people protect themselves when they feel threatened, and a skilful listener adjusts for this. Tips: listen openly and with empathy; practise supportive rather than one-way listening; ask for paraphrases and repetitions; listen between the lines; neither control the conversation nor interrupt; don't react to emotional words but interpret their purpose; don't judge before you comprehend. Good listening helps solve problems and see the world through others' eyes. Native American proverb: 'Listen or your tongue will keep you deaf.'

readings.title: The history of writing
readings.summary: People have been writing for over 5,000 years. Around 3000 BCE in Mesopotamia (between the Tigris and Euphrates, home of Sumer, Assyria and Babylon) people used pictograms mainly for economic information (agriculture, finance). These became cuneiform symbols inscribed on clay with reeds; professional scribes wrote about daily (quotidian) life and trade. At about the same time hieroglyphics developed in Egypt. Around 1500 BCE Chinese scribes wrote on tortoise shells using characters similar to today's; each character represents a word, so people must learn thousands, and they traditionally write with brush and ink. The Phoenicians invented the alphabet (each letter = a sound). The Roman alphabet (26 letters) is an improved form of it, used in Europe for 2,000 years. Written Arabic, used since the 4th century CE, is the second most widely used alphabet; it is the basis of Malay, Urdu and Turkish, is written right to left, has 28 letters, and like Chinese is a precious art form.

readings.title: Mobile phones

Professor Ramesh Jain says phones will become dominant devices for CCC (communication, computing and content), the 'ultimate remote control of our life' - what George Gilder calls 'teleputers'.

lessons.summary: The Focus on page introduces the Kuwaiti poet and economist Sheikha Suad Mohammed Al-Sabah, one of her poems (translated by Dr Shihab Ghanem), and metaphors and similes. Project 2 guides students through planning and conducting a survey about the English language.

readings.title: Sheikha Suad Mohammed Al-Sabah
readings.summary: Born in 1942 in Kuwait into the ruling family, she graduated from the Faculty of Economics and Political Sciences at Cairo University in 1973 and obtained a doctorate in economics from the United Kingdom in 1981. She founded the Sheikha Suad Al-Sabah Publishing and Distribution House, published several poetry collections, established a literary prize carrying her name, and wrote hundreds of economic and political essays and articles. Her poetry has been translated into many languages, including English.

readings.title: Poem 'I could have done nothing' (translated by Dr Shihab Ghanem)
readings.summary: The speaker lists the easy life she could have chosen: doing, reading and writing nothing, seeking fame, fashion and travel, swallowing her tears and accepting oppression, and ignoring the sighs and cries of the oppressed. Instead she 'betrayed the law of the female' and chose to grapple with words - to write and speak out about injustice.

lessons.title: Literature Time: The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn (Mark Twain)
lessons.summary: An adapted version of Mark Twain's novel told by Huck Finn in six episodes. Huck escapes from a hut on the river and travels down the Mississippi on a raft with Jim, Miss Watson's servant, who has been falsely accused of stealing. They meet the feuding Grangerfords, two frauds called 'the king' and 'the duke', and finally Tom Sawyer, who helps 'rescue' Jim from the Phelps farm - only to reveal that Jim was already free.

characters.name: Huck Finn
characters.description: The narrator; a boy who hates being 'civilised', kind, honest at heart and loyal to Jim.

characters.name: Jim
characters.description: Miss Watson's servant; runs away after being falsely accused of stealing. The most honest man Huck has ever met; loyal and caring.

characters.name: Tom Sawyer
characters.description: Huck's imaginative friend who loves adventure stories and makes Jim's rescue unnecessarily complicated.

characters.name: Widow Douglas and Miss Watson
characters.description: Sisters who try to civilise Huck. In this version Widow Douglas makes Huck stay in a hut; Miss Watson accuses Jim, but later frees him in her will.

characters.name: Colonel Grangerford and Buck
characters.description: A fine family in a deadly feud with the Shepherdsons.

characters.name: The king and the duke
characters.description: Two frauds: the 'Duke of Bridgewater' (about 30, a printer and actor) and the 'late Dauphin, King Louis XVII' (about 70, bald). They trick people for money.

characters.name: Mary Jane Wilks
characters.description: Peter Wilks's daughter, whom the frauds try to cheat out of six thousand dollars.

characters.name: Aunt Sally and Uncle Silas Phelps
characters.description: Farm owners who think Huck is Tom Sawyer.

characters.name: Aunt Polly
characters.description: Tom Sawyer's aunt, who reveals the boys' real identities.

episodes.title: Episode One
episodes.summary: Huck lives with Widow Douglas and Miss Watson, who want to civilise him. Tom Sawyer's gang plays at being robbers, attacking 'Spanish merchants' that turn out to be a school picnic. After spilling salt (bad luck), Huck is sent to live in a hut across the river, made to do chores and given poor food. He cuts a hole with a saw, smashes the door to make it look like a robbery, and escapes by canoe to Jackson's Island. There he finds Jim, who ran away after Miss Watson accused him of stealing (Jim says she was the real thief). They take useful things from a floating house and find a raft.

episodes.title: Episode Two
episodes.summary: Hearing that men will search the island for Jim, they set off on the raft at night, passing St Louis, heading for Cairo, Illinois, where Jim would be safe. Huck tells two men searching for a runaway that his 'father' on the raft has smallpox; they back off and give him twenty dollars. A steamer smashes the raft. Huck stays with the Grangerfords, who are in a feud with the Shepherdsons nobody can explain. When Sophia elopes with a Shepherdson, a horrible fight breaks out. Jim, who has fixed the raft, reunites with Huck: 'there was no place like a raft'.

episodes.title: Episode Three
episodes.summary: Huck rescues two men who claim to be the Duke of Bridgewater and the King of France; Huck knows they are frauds but lets them think they've fooled him. The king collects eighty-seven dollars at a camp meeting by pretending to be a changed philosopher; the duke sells newspaper subscriptions and prints a poster offering $200 for Jim so they can travel by day. Their Shakespeare show fails in Arkansas, so they advertise 'The King's Camelopard' (LADIES AND CHILDREN NOT ADMITTED), cheat the audience three nights and escape before the angry crowd attacks with rotten eggs. The duke disguises Jim as a 'sick Arab' with a blue face.

episodes.title: Episode Four
episodes.summary: Learning that Peter Wilks has died leaving six thousand dollars, the king and duke pretend to be his brothers Harvey and William from England. The doctor sees they are frauds, but Mary Jane trusts them. Huck steals the money back and hides it in a box of Peter's books (screwed shut), then tells Mary Jane the truth. At the auction the real Harvey Wilks arrives; in the confusion Huck escapes to the raft, but the frauds catch up with them.

episodes.title: Episode Five
episodes.summary: The king sells Jim to Mr Phelps for forty dollars. Huck writes to Miss Watson but tears up the letter, remembering Jim's friendship. Aunt Sally Phelps mistakes Huck for Tom Sawyer. Tom himself arrives, agrees to help free Jim and pretends to be his brother 'William Thomson'. The townspeople tar and feather the king and duke - Huck almost feels sorry for them.

episodes.title: Episode Six
episodes.summary: Tom guesses Jim is in the hut because the food includes watermelon. He insists on a complicated, book-style rescue: digging with knives (then picks 'pretending they're knives'), a rope ladder, a diary on a shirt, spiders in the hut, and an anonymous warning letter that brings fifteen armed farmers. They escape to the raft, but Tom twists his ankle and needs a doctor; Jim gives up his freedom to help the doctor nurse Tom. Tom reveals that Miss Watson died two months earlier and freed Jim in her will - he wanted the adventure. Aunt Polly arrives and reveals the truth. Tom gives Jim forty dollars for being a good prisoner. Aunt Sally wants to adopt and civilise Huck, but he plans to run away again.

themes: Honesty versus fraud and greed (the king and the duke)
Conscience: Huck tears up the letter to Miss Watson
